lesson.title: REM Sleep: A Wide-Awake Brain in a Paralyzed Body
lesson.summary: REM sleep is the stage of the sleep cycle marked by rapid eye movements, vivid dreaming, and brain activity that closely resembles wakefulness, even as the body's muscles are actively kept still.
lesson.body:
Rapid eye movement sleep, universally known by its abbreviation REM, is the stage that follows the non-REM stages described in the previous section, and it earns its name from the quick, jerky movements of the eyes that can be observed beneath closed eyelids during this period. What makes REM sleep so scientifically fascinating, and why it is sometimes called paradoxical sleep, is the mismatch between what an EEG recording shows and what is actually happening to the sleeper. During REM, brain wave patterns look strikingly similar to those of an alert, awake brain, fast and low in amplitude, even though the person is deeply asleep and often difficult to rouse.

This intense cortical activity during REM corresponds closely with the experience of dreaming. While some dreaming can occur during non-REM stages, the dreams that arise during REM sleep tend to be the most vivid, emotionally charged, and narratively complex, featuring elaborate storylines, strong sensory detail, and often bizarre or impossible scenarios. Given how physically active the dreaming brain appears to be during REM, one might expect the body to be moving right along with it, acting out whatever is happening in the dream. Instead, the opposite occurs.

During REM sleep, structures in the brainstem, particularly within the pons, actively inhibit the motor neurons that control most of the body's skeletal muscles, producing a state called muscle atonia, essentially a temporary, deliberate paralysis. This is not a passive side effect but an actively maintained protective mechanism, preventing a sleeper from physically thrashing about, walking, or striking someone while their brain is generating a vivid internal drama. The muscles controlling breathing and eye movement are notable exceptions, which is precisely why the eyes remain free to dart around beneath closed lids even as the arms and legs stay still.

The importance of REM sleep becomes especially clear through two lines of evidence. First, when people are selectively deprived of REM sleep, for instance by being awakened each time they enter this stage, they tend to show REM rebound on subsequent nights, spending a larger than usual proportion of sleep time in REM once allowed to sleep normally again, as though the brain were compensating for a genuine biological deficit rather than simply losing time. Second, a real clinical condition known as REM sleep behavior disorder demonstrates what happens when the normal atonia mechanism fails. People with this disorder physically act out their dreams, sometimes violently, because the brainstem circuitry that should be paralyzing their muscles during REM is not functioning correctly, offering a vivid, if unfortunate, illustration of just how essential that inhibitory mechanism normally is.

REM sleep is also associated with important cognitive functions, including the consolidation of certain kinds of memory and emotional processing, building on the sleep architecture introduced earlier in this chapter. Far from being a passive or minor stage tacked onto the end of a sleep cycle, REM represents a distinctive and biologically essential brain state in which intense cortical activity, vivid subjective experience, and carefully controlled bodily stillness all occur together.
